summary: Specifies how to protect the Babel routing protocol with Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS). Babel has no built-in way to authenticate neighbours or protect messages, and this adds authentication, integrity, and confidentiality between neighbouring routers.

plainLanguage.summary: Babel is a routing protocol for networks that have no clear central structure, such as a collection of small routers. By itself it does not check who sent a message. RFC 8968 wraps Babel packets in DTLS, a version of TLS for datagrams, so that two neighbours can prove who they are and nobody can alter the routes they exchange.

subtitle: How Babel routers use DTLS to authenticate neighbours and keep their routing messages private and tamper-proof.

tldr.problem: The Babel routing protocol has no way to authenticate neighbours or protect the messages between them, so an attacker can send crafted messages that pull traffic toward the attacker or an under-resourced target.
tldr.mechanism: Babel nodes run DTLS on a separate UDP port, 6699. The node with the lower address acts as the DTLS client, all unicast Babel traffic is protected, and only plain Multicast Hellos travel in the clear.
tldr.outcome: Neighbours get mutual authentication, integrity, replay protection and confidentiality. The arrangement gives a single authentication domain, so any node with the right credentials can convey any routing information.

facts.label: DTLS client
facts.value: The node with the lower IP address

facts.label: Reordering limit
facts.value: Packets reordered by more than two IHU intervals are dropped

today: RFC 8968 is a Proposed Standard, published in January 2021. No RFC obsoletes it and no RFC updates it, so it is the defined way to protect Babel with DTLS; the alternative is Babel-MAC in RFC 8967.

sections.title: Why Babel Needs Protection
sections.content:
The Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966) contains no means to authenticate neighbours or to protect the messages sent between them. Because of that, an attacker is able to send maliciously crafted Babel messages that could lead a network to route traffic to the attacker or to an under-resourced target, causing denial of service. This document specifies a mechanism to prevent such attacks using Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) (RFC 6347).

Protecting Babel packets with DTLS means the mechanism inherits the features DTLS offers: authentication, integrity, optional replay protection, confidentiality, and asymmetric keying. It is therefore expected to be applicable in a wide range of environments.

There is another mechanism for securing Babel, MAC authentication for Babel, or Babel-MAC (RFC 8967). Babel-MAC offers only basic features: authentication, integrity and replay protection, with a small number of symmetric keys. A comparison of the Babel security mechanisms and their applicability is in RFC 8966. One point to keep in mind is that Babel over DTLS provides a single authentication domain, meaning that all nodes that hold the right credentials can convey any and all routing information.

DTLS supports several mechanisms by which nodes can identify themselves and prove possession of secrets tied to those identities. This document does not prescribe which to use; the details of identity management are left to deployment profiles of Babel over DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain Babel trusts whoever sends a packet. A neighbour on the same link can claim routes it does not have, or send a message that makes everyone else send their traffic somewhere else. Wrapping the packets in DTLS means each neighbour proves who it is before its routing messages are believed.

sections.title: Starting and Maintaining a DTLS Connection
sections.content:
Babel over DTLS requires some changes to how Babel operates. DTLS is a client-server protocol, while Babel is a peer-to-peer protocol, and DTLS can only protect unicast communication, while Babel packets can go to both unicast and multicast destinations.

All Babel over DTLS nodes MUST act as DTLS servers on a given UDP port and MUST listen for unencrypted Babel traffic on another UDP port, which MUST be distinct from the first. The default port for Babel over DTLS is registered with IANA as the babel-dtls port, UDP port 6699, and the port exchanging unencrypted Babel traffic is the babel port, UDP port 6696.

When a node discovers a new neighbour, generally by receiving an unencrypted multicast Babel packet, it compares the neighbour's IP address with its own, using network byte ordering. If a node's address is lower than the neighbour's address, it acts as a client and connects to the neighbour. The node with the lowest address is therefore the DTLS client for that pairwise relationship. The node acting as client initiates the DTLS connection from an ephemeral UDP port, and nodes SHOULD ensure that new client connections use different ephemeral ports from recently used connections so that servers can tell a new connection from an old one. Alternatively, nodes could use DTLS connection identifiers as a higher-entropy mechanism.

When a node receives a new DTLS connection, it MUST verify that the source IP address is either an IPv6 link-local address or an IPv4 address belonging to the local network, and it MUST reject the connection if it is neither. Nodes use mutual authentication, so clients MUST authenticate servers and servers MUST authenticate clients. Implementations MUST support authenticating peers against a local store of credentials, and if either node fails to authenticate its peer it MUST abort the handshake. Nodes MUST only negotiate DTLS version 1.2 or higher, and MUST use DTLS replay protection to prevent attackers from replaying stale information. Nodes SHOULD drop packets that have been reordered by more than two IHU, or I Heard You, intervals, so that attackers cannot make stale information last longer. If a node receives a new DTLS connection from a neighbour to which it already has a connection, it MUST NOT discard the older connection until it has completed the handshake of the new one and validated the peer's identity.

To reduce the number of octets the handshake takes, Babel peers can use raw public keys or the Cached Information Extension, which avoids transmitting the server's certificate and chain when the client has cached that information from a previous handshake. TLS False Start can reduce round trips by allowing the second flight of messages to carry the encrypted Babel packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbours compare IP addresses, and the one with the lower address opens the connection. Both sides then check the other's identity against credentials they already hold, and the connection is dropped if that fails. Only DTLS 1.2 or later is allowed, and a node throws away a connection that has gone quiet for long enough.

sections.title: What the Protection Covers on the Wire
sections.content:
Babel over DTLS sends all unicast Babel packets protected by DTLS. The entire Babel packet, from the Magic byte at the start of the Babel header to the last byte of the Babel packet trailer, is sent protected.

When sending packets, Babel over DTLS nodes MUST NOT send any TLVs over the unprotected babel port, with the exception of Hello TLVs without the Unicast flag set. They MUST NOT send any unprotected unicast packets. This ensures the confidentiality of the information in Babel packets, such as the network topology, by only sending it encrypted by DTLS. Unless some out-of-band neighbour discovery mechanism is available, nodes SHOULD periodically send unprotected Multicast Hellos so that new neighbours can be discovered. To maintain bidirectional reachability, nodes can either rely entirely on unprotected Multicast Hellos, or send protected Unicast Hellos in addition to them.

Because only unicast packets are protected, an implementor can take an existing Babel implementation and replace any TLV previously sent over multicast with a separate TLV sent over unicast for each neighbour, keeping the same contents, except for Hellos as described above. Some implementations could also change the contents of IHU TLVs when converting to unicast, to remove redundant information.

On reception, a node can receive Babel packets either protected over a DTLS connection or unprotected over the babel port, and unprotected packets are treated differently. Nodes MUST silently ignore any unprotected packet sent over unicast. When parsing an unprotected packet, a node MUST silently ignore all TLVs that are not of type Hello, and MUST also silently ignore any unprotected Hello with the Unicast flag set. Receiving an unprotected packet can still be used to discover new neighbours, even when all TLVs in that packet are ignored.

It is RECOMMENDED that nodes associate the state of their DTLS connection with their neighbour table. When a neighbour entry is flushed from the neighbour table, its associated DTLS state SHOULD be discarded, and the node SHOULD send a DTLS close_notify alert to the neighbour if it believes the link is still viable.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole Babel packet is encrypted, not just parts of it. The only thing sent in the clear is the periodic multicast Hello that says a node is here, so that new neighbours can find each other. Anything else that arrives unprotected is ignored.

sections.title: Running Protected and Unprotected Babel Together
sections.content:
Implementations MAY implement both Babel over DTLS and unprotected Babel, and a node MAY simultaneously run both. A node running both MUST ensure that it runs them on separate interfaces, because the security properties of Babel over DTLS rely on ignoring unprotected Babel packets other than Multicast Hellos. An implementation MAY offer configuration options that allow unprotected Babel on some interfaces but not others, which effectively gives nodes on that interface the same access as authenticated nodes. That SHOULD NOT be done unless the interface has a mechanism to authenticate nodes at a lower layer, such as IPsec.

If Babel over DTLS and unprotected Babel are both operated on the same network, the Babel over DTLS implementation will receive unprotected Multicast Hellos and attempt to initiate a DTLS connection. These connection attempts can be sent to nodes that only run unprotected Babel, and those nodes will not respond. Babel over DTLS implementations SHOULD therefore rate-limit their DTLS connection attempts, to avoid causing undue load on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can run the protected and the plain version of Babel at the same time, but only on different interfaces. On a shared network, a protected node will keep trying to reach plain nodes that never answer, so the attempts are rate-limited.

sections.title: Packet Size and the Interface MTU
sections.content:
Compared with unprotected Babel, DTLS adds header, authentication tag, and possibly block-size padding overhead to every packet. That reduces the size of the Babel payload that can be carried. This document does not relax the packet size requirements in Section 4 of RFC 8966, but recommends that DTLS overhead be taken into account when computing the maximum packet size.

Nodes SHOULD compute the overhead of DTLS depending on the ciphersuites in use, and SHOULD NOT send Babel packets larger than the interface maximum transmission unit minus the overhead of IP, UDP and DTLS. Nodes MUST NOT send Babel packets larger than the attached interface's MTU adjusted for known lower-layer headers, at least UDP and IP, or 512 octets, whichever is larger, but not exceeding 2^16 minus 1 adjusted for lower-layer headers. Every Babel speaker MUST be able to receive packets that are as large as any attached interface's MTU adjusted for UDP and IP headers, or 512 octets, whichever is larger. This reception requirement does not take DTLS overhead into account, because the peer may not be able to compute the overhead of DTLS and the packet may be fragmented by lower layers.

Distinct DTLS connections can use different ciphers, which can have different amounts of per-packet overhead. The MTU to one neighbour can therefore be different from the MTU to another neighbour on the same link.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption costs extra bytes on every packet, so a router has to send smaller Babel packets than it would otherwise. The rule is the interface's MTU minus the headers for IP, UDP and DTLS, and never below a floor of 512 octets.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious client might attempt to perform a high number of DTLS handshakes with a server. Since clients are not uniquely identified by the protocol until the handshake completes, and can be obfuscated with IPv6 temporary addresses, a server needs to mitigate the impact of such an attack. Attackers might also try to keep in-progress handshakes open for as long as possible, using a variant of the attack commonly known as Slowloris. Mitigating these attacks might involve limiting the rate of handshakes from a given subnet, or more advanced denial-of-service avoidance techniques beyond the scope of this document.

Babel over DTLS allows Multicast Hellos to be sent unprotected, so attackers can tamper with them. For example, an attacker could send erroneous values for the Seqno and Interval fields, causing bidirectional reachability detection to fail. While implementations MAY use Multicast Hellos for link quality estimation, they SHOULD also emit protected Unicast Hellos to prevent this class of denial-of-service attack.

DTLS protects against an attacker who replays valid packets, but it cannot detect an active on-path attacker who intercepts valid packets and resends them at a later time. That attack could be used to make a node believe it has bidirectional reachability to a neighbour even though that neighbour has disconnected from the network. To prevent it, nodes MUST discard the DTLS state associated with a neighbour after a finite time of not receiving valid DTLS packets, for example when that neighbour's IHU timer fires. Relying solely on the receipt of Hellos is not sufficient, because Multicast Hellos are sent unprotected. An attacker could also save some packets and replay them later in the hope of propagating stale routing information, which is mitigated by discarding received packets that have been reordered by more than two IHU intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: Two attacks remain. A flood of half-finished handshakes can tie up the server, so the rate of new connections should be limited. And the plaintext multicast Hello can be forged to break the reachability check, so a node should also send its Hellos over the protected connection and should forget a neighbour it has not heard from in a while.
